idiom_name: property setter nulls a cached field; the getter recomputes once
implementation_notes: The property is the natural choke point: the setter updates the backing field and invalidates the cache, and the getter rebuilds it only when the slot is empty - the classic structure collapses into ordinary property code. A nullable cache field doubles as the dirty flag (null = out of date), which is concise but only safe when the derived value cannot legitimately be null; otherwise keep a separate bool. There is no BCL equivalent for an invalidatable value: System.Lazy<T> and LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized compute exactly once and cannot be reset, so they replace lazy initialisation, not this pattern.
pitfalls: `Lazy<T>` cannot be invalidated and caches factory exceptions: wrapping mutable source data in it pins the first computed value (and its first failure) forever.
Mutation through a contained reference (a List<T> field, a child object) never runs the property setter, so invalidation must live in the method that owns that mutation.
A nullable cache slot cannot represent a legitimately null derived value; use a separate bool or a sentinel when null is a valid result.

The recomputation may throw (I/O, parse): if the cache was cleared before the rebuild, a failure leaves the object dirty (good), but a caller that assumed success can observe an exception on a property read.

variants.name: volatile flag with lock-guarded republication
variants.idiom_name: volatile cache field plus lock in the slow path
variants.implementation_notes: For objects shared between threads the flag and the cache must be published in a defined order: a volatile reference field gives the acquire/release pair for the fast read, and the rebuild itself runs under a lock with a second check so only one thread computes. Microsoft's own guidance is that volatile is easy to misuse and that Interlocked, lock or the Volatile class provide clearer and stronger guarantees; use volatile only for the fast-path test and keep the rebuild and the cache assignment inside the critical section. If the value only needs one-shot initialisation, Lazy<T> is the safer replacement.
pitfalls: volatile only orders accesses to that field - it gives no atomicity for the recomputation and no mutual exclusion, so the rebuild still needs lock/Interlocked.
volatile cannot be applied to long/double fields (reads and writes are not guaranteed atomic) and cannot be used for locals.
Publishing a mutable cache object through a volatile reference does not safely publish its fields; build the value fully (ideally immutable) before the assignment.
The double-checked form must re-read the field inside the lock and return the local copy, or two threads can rebuild and the second assignment can throw away the first.

variants.name: WPF invalidation (framework-owned dirty flag)
variants.idiom_name: InvalidateVisual / InvalidateProperty instead of a hand-written flag
variants.implementation_notes: On WPF the element itself carries the dirty state: InvalidateVisual invalidates the rendering and forces a complete new layout pass, with OnRender called after the layout cycle, and InvalidateProperty/InvalidateMeasure do the same for dependency-property values and arrangement. The framework owns the flag, the recomputation scheduling and the batching, so application code only marks - the classic structure is replaced by a framework call. Microsoft's remark that InvalidateVisual is not generally called from application code is the caveat: framework elements already invalidate themselves when their visual tree or dependency properties change, and calling it by hand is for advanced cases such as a PropertyChangedCallback that influences layout.
pitfalls: WPF's dirty machinery is thread-affine: InvalidateVisual and InvalidateProperty must be called on the dispatcher thread, so background computation must publish into a Freezable or marshal before invalidating.
InvalidateVisual invalidates rendering and arranges a whole layout pass - marking in a hot loop (every mouse move) turns a targeted cache into a layout storm; coalesce the calls.
Dependency-property callbacks only fire for property changes, not for in-place mutation of a collection or a referenced object, so observable collections and immutable values are the safe shapes.
A hand-written bool flag next to dependency properties duplicates framework state and is easy to desynchronise; let the element's own dirty state be the single source.
